title: Lecture #10: How Arrays work in Java

questions.question: After `int[] arr = new int[5];` executes inside `main`, which description of memory matches the lecture?
options: The five ints live on the stack inside `arr`, exactly like `int x = 4;` holds 4 directly
`arr` is a reference variable on the stack; the five-int array object is created on the heap and `arr` holds its address
Both `arr` and the five ints are on the heap; the stack only stores the method name
`arr` is on the heap and points back to five int slots reserved on the stack
questions.explanation: A primitive local like `int x = 4` directly holds its value, but an array is a non-primitive: `new` creates the array object on the heap and `arr` (a stack local) only stores a reference to it. The tempting first option confuses arrays with primitives; `arr` does not directly hold the array.

questions.question: Why can Java read `arr[3]` of a one-million-element `int[]` just as fast as `arr[0]`?
options: The JVM walks from index 0 but skips elements in large jumps of 1000
The JVM keeps a hidden hash table that maps every index to its value
Elements are stored contiguously with equal size, so the address is computed directly as base address + (element size * index)
Arrays are always fully copied into the CPU cache when they are created
questions.explanation: Because all elements are the same size and stored back-to-back, the address of `arr[i]` is a single calculation: base + size * i. That is what 'random access' means, so no traversal is needed. Hashing or walking from the start would make access cost depend on something other than this one formula.

questions.question: What happens when this code runs?
options: Prints 50, then throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
Prints 40, then prints 50
Prints 50, then prints 0 (the slot after the array)
Fails to compile because `arr.length` cannot be used as an index
questions.explanation: Valid indices are 0 to length-1, so `arr[4]` prints 50 and `arr[5]` throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at run time. Java checks every access instead of reading whatever memory sits after the array, so it never prints a garbage or zero value (unlike unchecked languages).

questions.question: In a memory diagram, a `double[] d` starts at base address 500. Using the lecture's formula, at which address does `d[3]` begin?
questions.explanation: A double is 8 bytes, so the address is 500 + (8 * 3) = 524. 512 is what you get if you wrongly use the 4-byte int size; 503 ignores element size entirely, and 532 is the address of `d[4]`.

questions.question: What does the lecture say about the size of a `boolean`, for example in `new boolean[5]`?
options: The Java Language Specification fixes boolean at exactly 1 bit, so 8 booleans share one byte
The official Java docs do not fix a size; HotSpot (Oracle/OpenJDK) uses 1 byte per element, since memory is byte-addressed and this keeps base + (1 * i) simple and fast
A boolean is always 4 bytes because it is stored as an int internally in every JVM
A boolean takes 2 bytes, the same as a char, because true/false are stored as characters
questions.explanation: The notes point out that the official docs leave boolean's size unspecified, and HotSpot uses 1 byte per boolean-array element for better CPU efficiency (each element gets its own addressable byte). The '1 bit fixed by the spec' option is the common misconception: the spec only defines the values true/false, not a bit-level size.

questions.question: A teammate writes their own bounds guard for an array of length 5: `if (index < 0 || index > arr.length) throw new ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException();`. Which index gets past this guard even though it is invalid?
questions.explanation: Valid indices are 0..4, so the correct check is `index >= arr.length`. With `>`, index 5 (equal to the length) passes the guard even though it is one past the last element. -1 and 6 are still caught, and 0 is a valid index.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: Compile error: a row of an int[3][4] cannot be replaced
questions.explanation: `new int[3][4]` is an array of 3 references, each pointing to a separate int[4]. `arr[1]` is just one of those references, so it can be pointed at a new int[2]; lengths are then 3, 4 and 2. Thinking of a 2-D array as one fixed 3x4 block of 12 ints leads to the wrong '3 4 4' or '12' answers.

questions.question: A learner argues: "`String[] names = {"Aditya", "Abhay", "Rohit"};` can't support base + size * i addressing, because the names have different lengths." What is the correct reply?
options: Right, so String arrays are searched element by element from index 0
Right, so Java pads every string to the length of the longest one
Wrong, because Java stores all strings in a single char[] and indexes by character
Wrong, because the array holds equal-sized references to String objects stored elsewhere on the heap, so names[1] is at base + (reference size * 1)
questions.explanation: The array slots hold references (4 bytes in the lecture's diagram), not the characters, so every slot is the same size and the formula still works (e.g. 400 + 4 * 1 = 404). The actual "Abhay" object lives elsewhere and is reached through that reference. Padding or linear search is unnecessary.

questions.question: Trace which inner array each outer slot refers to. What does this print?
questions.explanation: `row` refers to the same inner array as `grid[0]`, so `row[1] = 7` makes it [0, 7]. `grid[1] = row` makes both outer slots point to that one inner array, so `grid[1][0] = 3` changes it to [3, 7], seen through both rows. Answers like '0,7,3,0' assume assignment copies the row, but it only copies the reference.

questions.question: For `int[][] arr = new int[3][4];` the outer array starts at 100 and its slots hold the row addresses 200, 300 and 400 (references are 4 bytes). How is the address of `arr[2][3]` found, as shown in the lecture?
options: Read the reference at 100 + 4*2 = 108, which gives 400; then the element is at 400 + 4*3 = 412
One step: 100 + 4*(2*4 + 3) = 144, because all 12 ints are stored contiguously
Read the reference at 100 + 4*3 = 112; then the element is at 112 + 4*2 = 120
Read the reference at 108, then the element is at 108 + 4*3 = 120
questions.explanation: Java's 2-D array is an array of arrays: first base + 4*i locates the row reference (108, holding 400), then that row's base + 4*j gives the element (412). The single-formula answer 144 assumes C-style row-major contiguous storage, which is not how Java lays out rows. The last option wrongly adds j to the slot address instead of the row's own base address.
